In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the scaling of anaerobically produced energy is not a simple linear relationship with size.
larger rainbow trout are more powerful swimmers than smaller trout.
the scaling of burst and sustained swimming performance in rainbow trout is not a simple matter, but is a function of the scaling of both aerobic and anaerobic muscle metabolism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the scaling of anaerobically produced power is limited by the scaling of anaerbiosis in the white muscle.
large trout can produce more lactate and red muscle than small trout, but that the power requirements for burst swimming are greater than the capacity to sustain anaerobic metabolism.

the scaling of burst swimming performance is not simply a consequence of the size of muscle fibres or the amount of anaerobic metabolic capacity, but is the product of a complex interaction among the size and mass-specific metabolic capacities of red and white muscle, the mass and size-specific power requirements of the fish, and the scaling of the red muscle mass.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the scaling of muscle power output is complex and cannot be predicted by simple allometric scaling of muscle mass or metabolic capacity.
the scaling of burst performance with fish size is more complex than previously thought.
there is a significant scaling of both the aerobic and anaerobic metabolic capacities in rainbow trout.
